references.text: Jesus' parallel teaching in the Sermon on the Mount that every tree is known by its fruit—you do not pick grapes from thornbushes or figs from thistles. This is the closest parallel to Luke 6:44.
Jesus says that a tree is known by its fruit, expressing the same principle that a tree is judged by what it bears.
James uses the same image: a fig tree cannot bear olives, and a vine cannot bear figs—a tree bears fruit according to its kind.
The fruit of the Spirit is described as good fruits of love, in contrast to the deeds of the flesh—an expression of the principle that inner life shows itself in outward fruit.
After the fall, God cursed the earth so that it would bear thorns and thistles—a background for the image of thorns as something unfruitful and negative.
Isaiah's parable of the vineyard where God expected good fruit but received only wild grapes—illustrates the principle that what grows reveals the roots.
Jeremiah says that the people have sown wheat but harvested thorns—an image of how the result reveals the spiritual condition.
The immediate context: a good tree does not bear bad fruit, and a bad tree does not bear good fruit—the basis for the statement in verse 44.
The subsequent application: a good person brings forth good from the good treasure of the heart, and an evil person brings forth evil—the fruit metaphor applied to the human heart and speech.
